title: Proseminar in History and Theory of Religion
description: Critical analysis of the key themes and figures in modern philosphy and psychology of religion, with attention to their role in the emergence and current practice of religious studies. Includes the works of such figures as Spinoza, Hume, Kant, Hegel, Marx, Nietzsche, Heidegger, Wittgenstein, Freud, and Jung.

title: Religion and the Body
description: The seminar explores the contributions of scholarship on the body in religion to re-visioning theories of the body from the methodological perspective of the history of religions. We will examine three areas of scholarship that have had a significant influence on contemporary theories: the body in philosophy, the body in social theory, and the body in feminist and gender studies. We will critically interrogate the limitations of these Western theoretical models through an analysis of categories and models of the body that are grounded in the distinctive idioms of non-Western religious traditions, with a focus on six modalities: ritual bodies, ascetic bodies, gendered bodies, sexual bodies, tantric bodies, and devotional bodies.

title: Proseminar in the History and Theory of Religion
description: Critical analysis of key themes and figures in phenomenology and history of religions, with attention to their role in the emergence and current practice of religious studies. Includes the works of such figures as Otto, van der Leeuw, Pettazzoni, Wach, Eliade, W.C. Smith, Smart, Long, J.Z. Smith, and Licoln.

title: Proseminar in the History and Theory of Religion
description: Critical analysis of key themes and figures in contemporary critical theory and cultural studies, with attention to their role in the current practice of religious studies. Includes the works of such figures as Benjamin, Foucault, Bourdieu, Derrida, Lacan, Kristeva, Butler, and Taussig.

title: Religion & Image
description: Icons. idols, visions: In many cases, across traditions, images give form to Religious Experience. Questions of visual representation and recognition are central to religious studies. This proseminar will ground students in core texts that theorize visual forms and artifacts in religious life ad related fields of social practice. We will study historical and contemporary contributions from aesthetics, psychoanalysis, and semiotics, alongside other approaches that have shaped the course of inquiry in art history, film studies and anthropology. The syllabus will also highlight visual relations as prescribed and debated within cultic contexts, most notably among Christians and Hindus.

title: Phenomenology of Love
description: In light of debate about the presence or absence of love in Martin Heidegger's thought, this course focuses on Heidegger's atheist inheritance of the theological analyses of love developed in Saint Augustine of Hippo. In and through this focus on the influence of a major theologian from late Antiquity in one of late-modernity's single most influential philosophers (decisive to phenomenology, hermeneutics, deconstruction, and Foucauldian genealogical thought, among others) the course serves as an introduction to twentieth-century Continental philosophy that highlights not only that philosophy's relevance to the study of religion but also the relevance of religion to engagement with such philosophy.

title: Religion and Materiality
description: An overview of various approaches to understanding materiality in the context of religion and of human culture generally, including concepts of landscape and taskscape, object agency, the new materialism, and material culture as archive. Attention is devoted to issues of equitable representation, colonialism and its effects, and ethical practices for the retrieval, possession, curation, and presentation of cultural objects.

title: Religion & Nature
description: This course critically examines the roles played by "religion" and "nature," within the context of North American cultural and environmental history. It will examine the contested ways in which religion and nature are understood, drawing on diverse sources and methodologies, and primary texts written by central figures in the field, both past and present. Specific topics include the origin and evolution of nature-religions and nature spirituality, religious naturalism, "greening of religions," and resistance to nature-inspired environmentalism. Students will gain a broad acquaintance with theoretical foundations, pivotal figures, social movements, etc.

title: Religion & Politics
description: This seminar adopts a history of longue durée to examine the mutual embeddedness of religion, politics, and the state across archaic, medieval, and modern social formations across the globe. It combines theoretical writings (Lefebvre, Foucault, Rappaport, Mahmood, Taylor, Lefort, Deleuze, and Guattari) with empirical analyses of religious politics in archaic states (Angkor, Inca, China, Aztecs, and Abrahamic religions). It explores religious movements in modernity in Korea, China, Mexico, Russia, India, and the US. Themes include ritualization of politics and states, gender politics, millenarianism, spatialization, "political theology," biopolitics, etc.

title: Religion and Environment
description: This seminar confronts the oppositions that helped launch modernity and the Anthropocene: Nature vs. Culture, and Religion vs. Science. Readings explore (re-)constructing, reconciling, and hybridizing religious environmentalisms in dialogue with modern science for our multispecies planetary flourishing. Issues and topics include: Anthropocene and Capitalocene; religious ontologies and environmental ethics; modern mechanistic science and an inert non-agential nature; human-animal-deity relationships; new animism; Gaia Theory; deep time; Asian religions as contrasted with Abrahamic religion. Theorists include Donna Haraway, Arne Naess, Bruno Latour, Philippe Descole, Viveiros de Castro.

title: Race & Religion
description: This seminar interrogates the concept of "race" as an essential category of analysis for the study of religion. The genealogy of "race" as co-constitutive with "religion" in the west is considered. The course also examines adjacent concepts marking perceived bodily differences and hierarchical social arrangements including "ethnicity," and "caste," as well as linked forms of identity (class, sex, gender). The course includes discussions of how race continues to inform and influence the profession.

title: Secularism
description: Surveys the 21st-century debates over secularism and locates them within a longer history of advocacy and critique. Students learn to distinguish among the various meanings of secularism and the secular, such as the separation of church and state, a philosophy with a this-worldly focus, religion-making, and the absence of religion. Students also consider whether secularism should continue to be a logic of governance, or if the contemporary critique of secularism has rendered it obsolete.

title: Spirituality
description: Explores the history and variety of the metaphysical tradition, which is often called "spirituality" in the U.S. and other parts of the world. Though this tradition can stand alone, it often blends with established religions and is sometimes lumped with nonreligion. Readings are primary sources, and they reflect the tradition's diversity. The range of sources shows that metaphysical spirituality's various manifestations share common roots and reflects metaphysical eagerness to appropriate from non-western cultures. Students will learn to recognize a tradition that remains subterranean despite its broad and varied influence.

title: Religion and Time
description: Explores the phenomenology of the lived experience of time as it has been mediated by various religious cultures. Topics to be discussed include myths of creation and the engendering of the cosmological time of the past; revelation as the diremptive disruption of the present; messianic eschatology and the redemptive narrativization of the linear circularity of the future; ritualization of time and the cultivation of individual and communal memory; the interface between holy and mundane in the theo-politicization of space and time; the dialectical sense of the profane.

title: Tradition
description: Centering the category tradition, students theorize ways the concept has been announced and enacted in three overlapping spheres: religious contexts, academic debates, and law. We engage classical theories of continuity and change, recent theorizations of invention, articulation, discursive tradition, and contemporary examples of scholars and activists reclaiming the category. Adjacent conceptual terrain to be covered includes discourses of orthodoxy and authenticity. The course is driven in part by examples from students research areas (e.g., ancestral invocations or the asserted status of sacred texts) in the service of our shared project to theorize claim-making about the standing of the past in the present.

title: Core Issues in the Study of Religion
description: Introduces graduate students to core issues in modern studies of religions and other world views.

title: Muslim Diasporas and Law
description: Examines the legal and social issues raised by the presence of Muslims in contemporary Western Europe and the United States. Civil rights, accommodation, and the construction of a dichotomy between moderate Islam and Islamism will be discussed.
prerequisites_raw: Graduate standing or professor approval. Graduate students will have additional readings and extra meetings with professor.

title: Sacred Texts of Major Religious Traditions
description: Introduction to the sacred primary texts of major religious traditions in English translation to encourage a comparative and pluralistic perspective. Emphasis is on the hermeneutics of reading, historical context and modern continuities, and relations between primary texts and modern Western theory.

title: Anthropology of Religion and Modernity
description: Survey of major works in the anthropology of religion, including Turner, Geertz, Comaroffs, Rappaport, Asad, Mahmood, Taussig, etc. Topics include nationalism, the state, gender, sexuality, colonialism, pilgrimage, ritual, media, globalization, conversion, and the public sphere. Ethnographies of diverse religious cultures are also included.

title: Religious Literature in Greek
description: Selected readings in both Christian and polytheist texts.
